id: Poem to Some of My Recent Poems

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My beloved little billiard balls, my polite mongrels, edible patriotic plums, you owe your beauty to your mother, who resembled a cyclindrical corned beef with all the trimmings, may God rest her forsaken soul, for it is all of us she forsook; and I shall never forget her sputtering embers, and then the little mound. Yes, my little rum runners, she had defective tear ducts and could weep only iced tea. She had petticoats beneath her eyelids. And in her last years she found ball bearings in her beehive puddings, she swore allegiance to Abyssinia. What should I have done? I played the piano and scrambled eggs. I had to navigate carefully around her brain’s avalanche lest even a decent finale be forfeited. And her beauty still evermore. You see, as she was dying, I led each of you to her side, one by one she scorched you with her radiance. And she is ever with us in our acetylene leisure. But you are beautiful, and I, a slave to a heap of cinders.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: God, Yes, She

outputs.L1:
My beloved little billiard balls, my courteous mongrels, my edible patriotic plums—you owe your beauty entirely to your mother, who resembled nothing so much as a cylindrical corned beef adorned with all the trimmings. May God rest her forsaken soul, for it was all of us whom she forsook; and I shall never forget her sputtering embers, nor the small mound that followed.

Yes, my little rum runners, her tear ducts were defective, and she could weep only iced tea. She wore petticoats beneath her eyelids. In her final years, she discovered ball bearings nestled in her beehive puddings, and she pledged her allegiance to Abyssinia. What was I to do? I played the piano and scrambled eggs. I had to tread with the utmost care around the avalanche of her mind, lest even a decent finale be forfeited to us. And still, her beauty endured, evermore.

You understand, then, that as she lay dying, I brought each of you to her side, one by one, and she scorched each of you with her radiance. She remains with us still, in our acetylene leisure. But you—you are beautiful, while I remain a slave to a heap of cinders.
outputs.L2: My cherished little spheres of polished ivory, my courteous half-breeds, you sweet patriotic fruits fit for eating—your loveliness comes from your mother, a woman built like a rolled cut of preserved beef complete with garnish. May her abandoned spirit find peace, for it was she who abandoned us all. I will always carry the memory of her hissing coals, and afterward, that small heap of ash. Yes, my little smugglers of spirits, her tear ducts never functioned properly—only chilled tea could fall from her eyes. Underskirts lived tucked beneath her eyelids. Toward the end of her days, she discovered metal bearings hidden in her honeyed desserts, and she pledged her loyalty to Ethiopia. What choice did I have? I sat at the piano while scrambling eggs on the stove. I had to tread carefully through the landslide of her failing mind so that some proper ending might still be saved. Her beauty, though, persisted regardless. Understand this: while she lay dying, I brought each of you before her one at a time, and her brightness burned each of you in turn. She continues to dwell among us in our welding-torch idleness. Yet you remain lovely, while I am bound in servitude to a pile of ashes.
outputs.L3:
Listen to me, you billiard balls, you mongrels, you plums shining dark and sweet on the branch of what's left of our family—whatever beauty you carry in your faces, in the polish of your skin, in the ridiculous sweetness that somehow survived everything, you got it from her. Not from me. I want that understood. I have contributed nothing to this world but upkeep and worry. She is the one who put the shine on you.

She was strange, I'll admit that now, though I never said it while she lived. There was something of the corned beef in her, something dense and pink and pressed into shape by forces larger than herself, sealed up in her own casing. And her eyes—her eyes did not work like other eyes. When she cried, and she cried often toward the end, what came out was not the salt water you'd expect but iced tea, faintly sweet, faintly bitter, sliding down the creases of her face like she was weeping the only beverage her body had left to offer. I never questioned it. You don't question the tear ducts of the woman who made you.

Near the end, she lost her way in her own mind. She wandered rooms that weren't there anymore. She made pronouncements at three in the morning—declarations of loyalty to Abyssinia, an empire that hadn't existed by that name in decades, as if she'd appointed herself its last citizen, its final diplomat. I did not laugh. I wrote it down. I sat with her through the confusion because someone had to, because I had decided long before that this was mine to carry, the tending of her, the slow labor of loving something that no longer entirely knew itself. I fed her. I turned her in the bed. I answered to whatever name she called me by that day.

Before she went, I made sure of one thing: that each of you came to her, one at a time, and let her put her hand on you, or what passed for her hand by then, so that she could touch you once more before the light in her guttered out completely. I brought you in. I stood at the door and watched her bless you without knowing the words for blessing anymore, watched her fingers move over your faces like she was reading them, like she was memorizing what she'd made.

And this is the part I need you to hear: you are still beautiful. Look at you—shining, plum-dark, ridiculous and alive. Whatever she gave you, it took. It held. But I am not shining. I am what's left in the grate after the fire's gone through—ash, gray, formless, sifting through whatever's left of my own hands. She used up all her light making you glow like that, and there was none left over for me. I don't resent it. I only note it, the way you'd note the weather, the way you'd note that the corned beef of her, the iced tea of her, the Abyssinia of her, has gone out of the world and left you gleaming and left me only this—the residue, the smoke, the coming-apart that happens to a man once the person he loved most has finished loving him back.
outputs.L4:
My children, gather close now, though I know you have scattered to your separate corners of the world with your separate faces that are pieces of her face rearranged, and let me tell you about your mother, who was not like other mothers, who did not bake bread but concealed ball bearings in her puddings so that eating dessert became a kind of Russian roulette for the teeth, who wept not water but iced tea, sweetened, always sweetened, so that her sorrow left a sticky trail across the linoleum that the dog would follow for hours, confused about whether to mourn or celebrate.

She was ill in ways the doctors never had proper names for—they would furrow their brows and mutter about her blood pressure or her nerves, but none of them understood that she was slowly turning into weather, into a low-pressure system that moved through our house rearranging the furniture and the light. I fed her broth from a spoon shaped like a question mark. I combed her hair, which had begun, in her final years, to smell faintly of struck matches and old hymnals. I did this alone, you understand, while you were off becoming yourselves in distant cities, though I never held this against you, not truly, not in the marrow of things.

I want you to know that I brought each of you back, one by one, in the last days—not to say goodbye, exactly, for goodbye was never a word she recognized—but to witness. Yes, to witness. Because her final moments were radiant in a way that defies the ball bearings and the iced tea, in a way that made the sickroom glow like something holy, or nearly holy, or holy enough for our purposes. Each of you stood at that threshold and saw what beauty looks like when it burns down to its last inch of wick. You saw where you came from. You saw what you carry in your own faces, whether you know it or not, whether you admit it at dinner parties or not.

And now I remain, the keeper of what's left, a slave to a heap of cinders, sifting through the ash for whatever bright thing might still be salvaged—a button, a bone, a memory of her laugh which sounded, if you recall, like a drawer full of spoons falling down a staircase. I do this gladly. I do this because someone must. I do this, my children, because she asked nothing of me except everything, and I gave it, and I would give it again, cinder by cinder, until there is nothing left of me either but a small gray pile that the wind, if it is kind, might scatter toward wherever you are.
outputs.L5:
# She Said Yes to God

There's a story about faith that isn't often told this way—a story where "she" and "God" and "yes" intertwine into something transformative.

Consider a woman standing at a crossroads, uncertain, perhaps frightened. The weight of a decision presses on her, and in the quiet space between doubt and action, she finds herself speaking—not to another person, but upward, inward, to something larger than herself. She asks for guidance. She asks for strength. She asks, simply, to understand.

And then comes the answer, or perhaps just the courage to move forward as if an answer had come. She says yes.

Yes to uncertainty. Yes to the unknown path ahead. Yes to trusting that whatever force she believes shapes the universe—call it God, call it providence, call it the deep well of her own conviction—will not abandon her.

This yes is not passive. It is not resignation. It is the boldest word in her vocabulary, spoken with trembling hands and a steady heart. Throughout history, women have stood in this exact place—Mary at the annunciation, ordinary women in ordinary kitchens facing extraordinary choices, mothers, daughters, believers of every faith tradition who whispered their assent to something beyond their control.

She said yes not because she understood everything, but because she understood enough: that faith often means walking forward without seeing the entire staircase, trusting the first step will hold.

God, in this narrative, isn't distant or abstract. God is the presence she turns to in vulnerability, the silence that somehow speaks, the mystery that invites her yes rather than demanding it.

In saying yes, she becomes something more than she was—not because God needed her permission, but because her willingness transformed the moment into partnership rather than mere occurrence. Her yes mattered. It always does.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, absurdist monologue delivered by an eccentric parent figure addressing their children with strange, poetic epithets.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Gathering Hour

Come here, my little barometers of Tuesday. Come, my six spoons of unfinished weather.

I have called you here—all fourteen of you, though I know only nine were born and the rest simply accumulated, the way lint accumulates, the way regret accumulates in the pockets of a coat you meant to donate—I have called you here to speak of the ladder.

You know the ladder. It leans against nothing. It has always leaned against nothing, and yet your grandfather climbed it for forty years, humming the same three notes, and arrived somewhere. We never asked where. It is rude to ask a man where he arrives. It is like asking a cloud its social security number.

My little unwound clocks. My marmalade constitutionalists.

I did not have children so much as I *acquired weather systems* that occasionally needed sandwiches. This is not a complaint. A father can love the hurricane and still mop the floor after. This is called *maturity*, or possibly *drainage*.

Oh, don't look at me with your father's eyes, the ones I keep in the jar, the ones that blink on Wednesdays out of spite.

I want to tell you about the Rule. There has always been a Rule, though its wording changes depending on the moon's mood and whether the toaster has been fed. The Rule, as best I can translate it from the original Silence, is this: *never trust a door that apologizes.* A door that says "sorry" as you pass through it is a door planning something. I have seen it happen. Your Uncle Whistlebrick walked through such a door in 1962 and came out the correct height but the wrong decade.

You—yes, you, my soup-colored middle one, my algebra left out in the rain—stop trying to fix the epithet. It is not broken. It is *ripening.*

Someday you will all leave this house, this teetering hatbox of a house, and you will go into the wide brutal simple world where doors do NOT apologize and clouds have paperwork and nobody, *nobody*, will call you their little thimbleful of Thursday, their barefoot algebra, their last good cough before winter.

And in that moment—cold, official, forewarned—you will miss the ladder. You will miss that it went nowhere. You will understand, at last, in your bones, in the soft telegraph of your bones, that *nowhere was the whole point*, that I built you a childhood shaped like a question so that no answer could ever cage you.

Now eat your soup. It's listening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of experimental prose in the style of Gertrude Stein or Djuna Barnes, full of odd juxtapositions and dreamlike imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Room That Remembers Its Own Weather

There was a woman who kept a clock inside her mouth and when she spoke the hours fell out like teeth, small and white and ticking on the floor where the dog would not eat them. This is not that story. This is the story of the room.

The room had a window that opened onto another window, and that window opened onto a field, and the field was always the same field remembering itself, over and over, the way a bruise remembers the door.

Say the room. Say it again. The room is not the room when you say it twice, it becomes a sister-room, a room with the same furniture but arranged for grief instead of tea. The chairs sit differently when grief comes to visit. They lean.

There was a man in the corner who was made of Sunday. Not made *like* Sunday. Made *of* it — the slow gray taffeta of it, the church-bell nausea of it, the smell of boiled things. He did not move because Sunday does not move, it simply arrives and sits down inside whatever is nearest.

The woman with the clock in her mouth came into the room that was becoming its sister and she said, *I have swallowed the wrong hour again,* and nobody minded because time in that house was communal, like soup, like the disease that goes from cup to cup at Christmas.

Outside, the field was doing what fields do, which is wait with its mouth open for rain or for God, whichever arrives first wearing the right coat.

A bird came to the second window — not the first window, never the first, the first window was reserved for weather that had already happened — and the bird had the face of someone's grandmother, patient, disapproving, made of the kind of lace that itches.

*I have been meaning to leave this room,* said the man made of Sunday, though his mouth did not move, Sundays do not require mouths, they require only the slow accumulation of afternoon.

The clock-woman's teeth kept falling. The dog, still refusing, grew old in the corner, grew older than the corner, grew old enough to remember when the corner was a different shape, a shape with more room in it for sorrow, before sorrow got fat and had to be let out at the seams.

Rain began in the field which was also the window which was also, some said, the inside of the clock-woman's mouth, though this could not be proven, proof being another kind of furniture the room did not currently stock.

*Sit,* said Sunday, to no one, because Sunday only ever speaks to the furniture, and the furniture, being well-trained, obeyed, though it was already sitting, had never done anything else, would go on sitting through the war and the wedding and the long gray afternoon that swallowed both.

The bird at the window laughed like lace tearing.

This is not the end. The room does not end. It simply forgets what it was in the middle of, the way a sentence forgets its own beginning by the time it arrives, exhausted, wearing someone else's coat, at

the field again, the same field, remembering the same weather, the woman still losing hours through her teeth, small white hours, ticking on the floor,

and the dog, at last, bending down to eat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly comic eulogy-like speech about a deceased mother, mixing tenderness with bizarre, nonsensical descriptions.
counterfactuals.output:
# Eulogy for Margaret "Peggy" Holloway

Thank you all for coming. Mom would be touched by this turnout, though she'd also insist on knowing why the Hendersons brought a casserole when everyone knows she was allergic to sympathy in food form.

Margaret Holloway was, in the truest sense, a force of nature—specifically the kind of force that makes you evacuate a coastline. She raised four children, buried three husbands—no wait, that's not right, she buried one husband three times, which the coroner said was "logistically impressive" and "possibly illegal."

She had a laugh like a screen door in a hurricane, and she smelled perpetually of Chanel No. 5 and printer toner, because she believed the two scents "cancelled out the smell of lies." I never asked whose lies. I still don't know whose lies.

Mom taught me everything I know about resilience, mostly by example, but occasionally by hurling a phone book at my head when I complained about my day. She used to say, "Grief is just love with nowhere to send its mail," which is beautiful, and also something I'm pretty sure she read on a bathroom wall in Reno.

She had opinions about everything—the government, the neighbors, the correct way to fold a fitted sheet (there is none, she insisted; it's a scam invented by "the linen cartel"). She once fought a raccoon for the honor of the family and, as far as we know, won, though the raccoon has never been seen since and neither has our old cat, so.

In her final years, she took up beekeeping, not because she liked honey, but because she said the bees "understood her rage." I have her ashes here in an urn shaped like a lighthouse, because she once told me she wanted to "guide ships to their doom," and honestly, at this point, who am I to deny her?

She was tender in the way a cactus is tender—if you didn't get too close, and you wore gloves, and maybe long sleeves, you'd find something soft in there. She loved us fiercely, in her own way, which mostly involved yelling "I love you" from another room while the television was too loud for anyone to actually hear it.

Mom, wherever you are now—probably haggling with Saint Peter over the pearly gates' return policy—know that we love you. We miss your chaos. We miss your terrible advice. We miss the way you called every appliance "he" and every insurance agent "the enemy."

Rest, if you can. Though frankly, I doubt it. I imagine you're already reorganizing heaven's filing system and telling God his robe "makes him look like he's trying too hard."

We love you, Mom. Go haunt something proudly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness passage narrated by someone speaking to their "little ones," blending grief, love, and absurdist humor.
counterfactuals.output:
Little ones, come here, come sit, no not on the good chair, the good chair remembers your grandfather's weight and gets confused, furniture has feelings I've decided, I decided that this morning around four a.m. when I couldn't sleep and went downstairs to argue with the refrigerator about expiration dates, the yogurt said it was fine, I believed the yogurt, I believe most dairy products more than I believe most people at this point, is that wrong, little ones, tell me that's wrong.

Your grandfather used to say grief is just love with nowhere to go, and I used to think that was a lovely thing to cross-stitch onto a pillow, and now I think it's actually kind of a terrible design for a species, whoever built us should have to answer for this, love just piling up in the hallway like Amazon boxes, unopened, growing, until one day you trip over a box marked FEELINGS FRAGILE DO NOT SHAKE and it turns out to weigh four hundred pounds and also it's crying.

He's not dead-dead, little ones, I mean he is, he's the kind of dead where you still reach for the phone, my thumb still knows his number better than it knows my own social security number, my thumb is in mourning independently of the rest of me, my thumb needs its own casserole from the neighbors.

Is this too much for you. Tell me if this is too much. I'll switch to the thing about the raccoon, remember the raccoon, remember how it opened the cooler like it had read the manual, like it had a little raccoon MBA, business degree from Raccoon State, "Advanced Cooler Studies," and your grandfather laughed so hard he had to sit down on the actual ground, the actual dirt, a grown man on the ground laughing about a trash bandit's competence, and that's the last really good laugh I remember him having and I'm choosing to be furious about that instead of sad because furious has better posture.

Little ones. Little loves. Here's the absurd part, here's the part that makes me laugh in the church-quiet way where you're not supposed to laugh: at the funeral home they asked if we wanted him in his glasses. His glasses. As if where he's headed there's fine print. As if eternity has a lot of forms to fill out and he'll need to read the terms and conditions closely, "I agree to the everlasting," click accept, and I said yes, glasses on, because what if he needs to see how ridiculous we all look crying into little paper cups of bad coffee, what if the last thing he gets is a clear view of us being a mess, and honestly, little ones, I think he'd have loved that view best of all.

So here's your snack, here's your socks, here's your absurd, devastating mother telling you the world is soft and sharp at the same time, like a blanket made of little knives, cozy and dangerous, that's grief, that's Tuesday, that's love, eat your crackers, hold my hand, we're going to be fine, we're going to be a beautiful disaster, come here, come here, little ones, come here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of avant-garde flash fiction featuring strange metaphors (billiard balls, ball bearings, cinders) to explore themes of memory, loss, and inherited beauty.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Small Round Things

Grandmother kept her memories in a felt-lined box, arranged like billiard balls before the break—each one numbered, each one waiting for the cue that would send it spinning into darkness or light. *This is your mother at seven,* she'd say, tapping the eleven-ball, striped amber and cracked down the middle like an egg that dreamed of flying. *This is the war.* The eight-ball, obsidian, always sinking, always sinking.

I inherited the box when the felt had worn to threads. By then I understood: memory is not a photograph but a physics problem. Momentum. Collision. The way one recollection strikes another and sends it careening into a pocket you didn't know existed, gone, gone, only the felt-burn smell of where it used to be.

My mother's beauty came down to me like ball bearings, small and silver and precise, packed in Vaseline inside a tin that once held Danish butter cookies. *These kept the war machines turning,* she said, though she meant something else, something about how loveliness is just friction reduced to almost nothing—the exact tolerance between too much feeling and none at all. I have her cheekbones. I have her way of rolling grief between my palms until it grows warm and forgettable, a bearing spinning so fast it appears to stand still.

Cinders came later, after the house burned—not from fire but from cold, from the woodstove's slow exhale over sixty winters. I found them in the yard each spring: gray commas, small stopped sentences, the alphabet of everything my grandfather never said aloud. *Cinders are just wood that finished dying,* my mother told me, sweeping them into a coffee can. *Don't romanticize the ash.*

But I do. I romanticize the ash because the ash is honest in a way the billiard balls never were, in a way the ball bearings, spinning their frictionless lies, could never manage. The ash says: *something burned here. Something was warm enough to matter, once.*

I keep them all now—the cracked eleven-ball, the tin of bearings gone waxy with age, a mason jar of cinders that crumble to gray silk if you breathe on them wrong. I keep them the way you keep a language you'll never speak fluently, mouthing the shapes of words that meant *home* to someone else.

At night I hear them shifting in their drawers—click of ball against ball, whisper of metal sphere against metal sphere, the dry rustle of things that used to burn. This is inheritance: not the beauty itself but the residue of beauty's motion, the sound of loss still rolling, still finding new corners to disappear into.

Someday my daughter will open these drawers and ask what any of it means. I will not have an answer. I will only have the felt-burned box, the Vaseline tin, the mason jar—objects that stand in for the enormous, ungraspable thing itself, the way a cinder stands in for fire, the way a photograph stands in for a woman who is already, quietly, becoming smoke.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
